proposal.title: Levitsky Said a Slide Into Competitive Authoritarianism Was the Most Likely Outcome
proposal.short: NPR’s Steven Levitsky said the most likely outcome was a slide into competitive authoritarianism; this was his forecast, not a finding that it had occurred.
proposal.medium: In an April 22, 2025, NPR interview, Harvard professor Steven Levitsky said the “most likely outcome” was a slide into competitive authoritarianism. He described this as a forecast about democratic backsliding, not a finding that the United States had already completed that transition or ended constitutional government.
proposal.long: NPR’s Fresh Air interviewed Harvard government professor Steven Levitsky on April 22, 2025, about democratic backsliding under President Donald Trump. Asked what kind of autocracy the United States might become, Levitsky said the “most likely outcome” was “a slide into” competitive authoritarianism. He described such systems as retaining a constitution, regular elections, a legislature and a legal opposition, while abuses of power tilt competition against opponents. Earlier in the interview, NPR quoted Levitsky and coauthor Lucan Way’s Foreign Affairs article as saying U.S. democracy would likely break down during the second Trump administration under liberal-democracy criteria. Both statements are forecasts and analysis attributed to Levitsky and Way. They do not establish that the United States had already completed that transition, that constitutional government ended, or that permanent autocracy was established. NPR also records that their article defines liberal democracy using suffrage, free and fair elections, and broad protection of civil liberties.

source_to_fact_support.supports: Transcript dated April 22, 2025, identifies Levitsky as a Harvard government professor; he says the “most likely outcome” is a “slide into” competitive authoritarianism, describes those regimes, and quotes the coauthored Foreign Affairs forecast.
